lot_address.note: SEATED BY THE LOT-ADDRESS POLICY (docs/LOT-ADDRESS.md; liberty L216). The Lake Street notice prints a LOT AND A BLOCK — LOT No. 7, in block No. 16, one lot east of Haddock's Tavern, on Lake street, in the town of Chicago — which is the plat's own language and the strongest placement statement in the corpus; 6 printings, 1834-06-18 to 1834-11-19, 4 of them cited here as legible, claims chicago_democrat_1834_06_18#c006, chicago_democrat_1834_09_03#c005, chicago_democrat_1834_10_15#c006, chicago_democrat_1834_11_19#c010. THE ADDRESS IS WHAT THIS ROOF GAINS AND THE ONLY THING IT GAINS: its existence, its position, its footprint and every form value are the 665-roof programme's and are unchanged, its `function` still reads as the anonymous family the recipe dealt it, and no coordinate moved to seat this. THE NOTICE SAYS OF THIS LOT: a large dwelling-house; a fine well. The notice says 'There is on said lot a large Dwelling-House'. Four of the six printings carry the words unbroken. WHAT IS DRAWN AT THIS ADDRESS IS STILL NOT THIS HOUSE, and it now answers the word: the roof standing on the lot is the 665-roof programme's own count-unit, and T-0593 re-dealt it out of the D3 one-room cottage band into H1, 'Larger one-and-a-half-story house', at 8.03 x 9.96 m and one and a half storeys. H1 is the lowest rung the family crosswalk itself calls larger and calls a house, which is the whole of what this notice's adjective supports; the south district's remainder paid for the slot and the displaced D3 went back into it, so no total moved. Until 2026-09-04 the fabric was a 5.36 x 6.38 m one-room cottage and this note said the mismatch was stated rather than repaired. The ADDRESS is still what this record gains: existence, position, footprint and every form value stay conjectural and the grade does not move. docs/LOT-ADDRESS.md § 'When the notice describes the building' is the rule and L222 is the ruling. NOT DRAWN, and T-0592 has now settled why. The notice's second structure is a well and it is documented as plainly as the house; what was missing was a rule to place it by, and the reason recorded here used to be an absence — 'the town has no well' — which described the model rather than the town. THE READING IS docs/RESEARCH/wells.md AND ITS ANSWER IS NOT A WELL. Chicago in July 1835 took its drinking water from the lake by cart: the Board of Trustees paid $95.50 on 10 November 1834 for the digging of ONE public well, in Kinzie's Addition, and after that the town was served by two-wheeled carts carrying a hogshead, filled by pail at the foot of Randolph Street and run off at a customer's door through a short leathern hose at five to ten cents the barrel (town_findings_andreas_v1#c012, #c013); the Chicago Hydraulic Company was not chartered until 18 January 1836 and its works were not finished until 1842 (#c014). No ordinance of this town requires, sites or pays for a well — the fire ordinances of 1833, September and October 1834 and the code of 5 August 1835 legislate wardens, bystanders and a bucket line and never the water in the buckets. So there is no density to deal a well class from, and inventing one would misdescribe the town more badly than leaving it with none. THE WELL STAYS DOCUMENTED AND ABSENT, on that argument rather than on an absence. It is one of only three wells this project can name in a town of 3,265 people, and the fact that G. Spring advertised it in all six printings, beside the size of his house, is the argument that a well was a thing worth mentioning rather than a thing every lot had. The notice ends 'For terms enquire of G. SPRING' and says NOTHING ELSE about him. He is the man to apply to, which is not a statement that he owned the lot, and is certainly not a statement that he lived in the house — the same G. Spring is the attorney whose office the papers put second door west of the corner of Franklin and South Water. So this house is not named for him, and the register's business_g_spring is not moved here. T-0412 is the same trap read from the other side: a building offered FOR SALE must not mint a placement on its vendor. THE ADDRESS IS READ; WHERE THE ADDRESS LANDS IS THE BOTTOM TIER, and the chain is short enough to state in one breath. The words 'lot 7, block 16' are a direct reading of four printings. The block number is `inferred` — three blocks counted east of the one numeral the Wright sheet shows (data/traces/thompson_block_numbering.json). The lot number is `conjectural` twice over: four lots to a block face is a reading of one block, the lot lines it numbers are the plat module's and are drawn from no sheet, and the counter-clockwise scheme itself was read off block 18. A chain is as strong as its weakest link, so which committed roof stands at this address is graded at the bottom tier — the same grade the roof already carried, and it does not rise because a documented address was put on it.

persons.name: T. O. Davis
persons.note: A DOCUMENTED RESIDENT OF THE SCENE MONTH ITSELF - the American's first issue belongs to June 1835, weeks before 1 July, which makes this one of only three households in the parcel whose Chicago presence is fixed by an event inside the scene season. data/structures/chicago_american_office.json already carries him. FERGUS 1839'S LATER LISTS — 1837 AND 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 names this person 1 time in its two later lists: the poll of Chicago's first city election, 2 May 1837 — “T. O. Davis,” (f1839_v0104, printed page 42, ward 1, voting for John H. Kinzie). What a match may carry, and it is short: that the man was in Chicago on 2 May 1837 and in that ward. It is written as 1837 evidence with describes_date 1837-05-02, never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on this alone. Under the ratified ladder a second contemporary source is what lifts projected_resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not about July 1835. The ward is a location in the CITY of 1837, whose six wards are drawn on printed page 46; it is not a location in the town of 1835 and does not place a house. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Davis' folds to the same string as the 1837 entry's, and the given name of both begins T. (data/research/directories/fergus_1839_election_crosswalk_1835.json and fergus_1839_register_crosswalk_1835.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date — or a register four years after it — is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about July 1835. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

residents.research_note: THE NEWEST ARRIVAL IN THE PARCEL, and the one whose paper this project quotes most often for the state of the town in the scene year. A NOTE FOR ANY LATER PARCEL: the Chicago American of 1835-36 is the single most valuable unfetched source for this programme. Andreas quotes its advertisements by name and date - Frederick Thomas's drug and paint store of 8 June 1835, John Davis of the Steamboat Hotel among its first patrons, W. H. and A. F. Clarke's new drug store of 11 November 1835 - and every such advertisement is a documented resident with a trade and often an address, in the scene year rather than nineteen months before it.

persons.name: Elmira Fowler
persons.note: A DOCUMENTED PERSON, AND NOTHING ELSE IS CLAIMED. The papers name 'ELMIRA FOWLER' and give the trade; they do not say where this household lived, who else was in it, or when it came. So the record around this person carries nothing but the person: no dwelling, no division, no family, each written as unattested in its own block rather than filled in from the shape of the rest of the town. Cited at the Democrat of 5 November 1834, column 4. THE TOWN NEVER INVENTED A ROOF FOR THIS TRADE. The occupation census raised reconstructed households for the trades a town of 3,265 people needed and could not document; `dressmaker` was not one of them, which is why this person could only ever be ADDED and never seated on an existing record — data/research/newspapers/register_1835.json calls it `new_resident` for exactly that reason. No figure is drawn (docs/LIBERTIES.md L1). READ THROUGH A TRANSCRIPTION, not a scan: the owner's ruling of 2026-08-28 grades a transcription-mediated reading as documented, and the source record for the run states that standard and its limits. A scan read that confirms or corrects the name upgrades this entry. THE SECOND PRESBYTERIAN ROLL — A NAME ON A CHURCH LIST THAT OPENS IN 1842, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1892 printed membership roll of the Second Presbyterian Church of Chicago, read line by line into this repository, carries 1 line whose surname and given initial agree with this person's — “Fowler, Ellen | Profession. | October 31, 1879.” (second_presb_0019, printed page 155), admitted 1879-10-31 by profession. Under the rule that decided it: Surname 'Fowler' folds to the same string as the roll line's, and the given name of both begins E. WHAT THE MATCH MINTS OR REGRADES: “NOTHING. A line on a roll that opens in June 1842 cannot place a person in the town of July 1835, and this file makes no proposal that it does. What a match IS: the same surname and initial, in Chicago, within seven years — a lead for a later pass that is allowed to write people.” This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE: under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the roll is handed to the card as a thing a reader may weigh, and the verdict stays with T-0515, which applies the ladder against every source at once.

residents.research_note: MINTED FROM THE NEWSPAPER REGISTER (T-0376), AND THE HOUSEHOLD IS A CONTAINER RATHER THAN AN ARGUMENT. Every other record in this dataset argues for a household — a family the sources count, or a trade the town demonstrably needed. This one argues for a PERSON: the Democrat and the American name Elmira Fowler as a dressmaker at Chicago 1 time(s), and this reconstruction did not hold them. `data/residents/` has no way to carry a person except inside a household, so one was written around them and told to claim nothing: one member, no dwelling, no division, no origin, no arrival beyond the bound the paper sets. Reading a family, a house or a quarter of town into this record would be reading something the papers do not say. tools/mint_documented_residents.py derives the whole minted set and prints every candidate it refused, with the reason.

persons.name: Gurdon Saltonstall Hubbard
persons.note: ELECTED A TRUSTEE OF THE TOWN AT THE SECOND ELECTION, 11 AUGUST 1834 - 'J. H. Kinzie, G. S. Hubbard, E. Goodrich, J. K. Boyer, and John S. C. Hogan were chosen Trustees' - so he is on the board through the municipal year that ends in the scene month. He is also the man whose 1881 correction of the Wau-Bun view of Fort Dearborn supplies four of the constraints this project's fort dossier rests on: that the enclosure ran 'nearly north and south, east and west', that the north picket line stood nowhere more than 80 ft from the water, that the ground at the fort was 'not over eight feet above the River at its lowest stage', and that the north and south gates were on one sight line. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 2 times: Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Hubbard, Gurdon S.” (tax_1833_046, line 98); Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Hubbard, G. S.” (poll_1834_055, line 224). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Hubbard' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json). OLD SETTLERS, 1879 — A DATE THIS MAN GAVE FOR HIMSELF, AND STILL NOT A FACT ABOUT 1835. The Calumet Club's FIRST reception to the settlers of Chicago prior to 1840, 27 May 1879, printed its register in the proceedings (Early Chicago, Chicago, 1879, pages 84-90), and this man's entry reads “Hubbard, Gurdon S. | 1818, Oct. 1, | Windsor, Vt. | 76 | 243 White St., Chicago.” — name, his own date of arrival, his birthplace, his age and his 1879 post-office address, in the register's five columns. The date of arrival is HIS RECOLLECTION, set down forty to sixty years after the event; the address is where he lived in 1879 and is never read as an 1835 residence. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a later recollection corroborates, enriches and dates and cannot lift a rung by itself, so this record's GRADE IS UNCHANGED by it: T-0513 consolidates the identity and T-0515 regrades. Identity by rule OS1 — surname and spelled-out forename agree, one bearer (data/research/old_settlers/crosswalk.json). THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 5 times, as “HUBBARD GURDON S”, “HUBBARD GORDON S”, 1830-09-27 to 1833-10-22: 4 lots in the platted town — lot 1 of block 19 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L1BL19CHIOT, as printed); lot 2 of block 19 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L2BL19CHIOT, as printed); lot 7 of block 19 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L7BL19CHIOT, as printed); lot 8 of block 19 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L8BL19CHIOT, as printed) and 1 parcel of the school section — BL52 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), as read, 2.90 acres stated in all, for $293.00 (ls0239, ls1236, ls1237, ls1238, ls1239). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE SCHOOL-SECTION ROWS ARE GROUND INSIDE THE TOWN, NOT FARMLAND: section 16 of T39N R14E was platted and sold off by lot and by block at the sale of 1833, which is why the register states 0000.00 acres against most of them. Ground inside the town is nearer to this reconstruction than a quarter-section is, and it is still a purchase: the register names a purchaser and never an occupant, and nothing here puts this person on that ground. THE TOWN LOTS ARE THE PLAT ITSELF, AND THEY ARE NOT ACRES: Cook County's register describes them by lot and block in a platted town and gives them no section, no township and no acreage at all, so they add nothing to the acre figure above and $133.00 to the money. This project does not expand the register's town codes, so which addition a lot stands in is carried as the code and not as a name. It is still a purchase and it still places nobody. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: HUBBARD GURDON S matches Gurdon Saltonstall Hubbard: the forename names Gurdon Saltonstall Hubbard of the 5 people of this surname, and the forename agrees in full. (data/research/land_sales/resident_crosswalk.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE 1840 FEDERAL CENSUS — A HEAD FIVE YEARS AFTER THE SCENE, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1840 federal census of Chicago, read line by line off the left sheets in this repository, carries 1 head of this name — “Gurdon S. Hubbard” (33S7-9YYJ-W6, printed page 232, line 17). This project has ruled the head a MATCH for this person: the full name agrees, it is unique on both sides, and a discriminator independent of the name — directory persistence — separately places the same person in Chicago after the 1840 book was taken. Under the rule that decided it (L6 matched), by the crosswalk's own ladder (data/research/census_1840/resident_crosswalk.json). LATER EVIDENCE ONLY. The ratified grading ladder binds: an 1839 or 1840 appearance alone is never an 1835 resident, and 1840 household composition is never back-projected to the 1835-07-01 scene. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and an 1840 head is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

residents.research_note: THE OLDEST LIVING RESIDENT, AND THE ONE HOUSEHOLD IN THE PARCEL WHOSE ARRIVAL DATE THIS PROJECT HAD TO REFUSE TO GUESS - UNTIL A SENTENCE TURNED UP. Everything about Hubbard's later Chicago life was documented here and the date he first came was a fact everyone knew and nothing in data/sources/ stated, so it was carried as a conjecture citing nothing and left visibly empty rather than quietly filled: it was the case AGENTS.md rule 1 exists for. Hurlbut's American Fur Company chapter, read for T-0575 and cited by this record since T-0594, closes it - Montreal 13 May 1818, Mackinaw 4 July, Chicago the last day of October or the first of November - and the asymmetry that was worth leaving visible is now a smaller and more interesting one. The sentence is the COMPILER'S, not the man's: it stands outside the quotation marks in which Hubbard speaks four lines later, so a date this project had no source for at all now has a source of 1881 at rung 4, and the record says both things on its face rather than letting the citation look like an attestation. WHAT T-0753 ADDED, AND THE ONE THING IT COULD NOT. The same sentence carries more than the date T-0594 spent, and the rest of it is now on the card: `origin` reads "Windsor, Vermont, by way of Montreal" rather than the "Montreal" a careless reading of the field would have written, and the person carries a `birth_year` of 1802 with the birthplace in its note, both at the inferred grade the rung-4 layer supports and both corroborated by the man's own Calumet Club register entry of 1879. THE PARENTS WERE THE PART THAT DID NOT FIT, AND T-0849 RULED WHERE THEY GO. Hurlbut names Elizur and Abigail (Sage) Hubbard, and this dataset held no structure for them: the only relationship structure it has is the household-level `kin[]` block ratified on 2026-09-05, whose rows are reciprocal between two households IN THIS DATASET, and Hubbard's parents were living in Montreal, were never in this scene, and have no household here. T-0849 set out two readings - leave parentage outside the town as evidence, or invent an external kin row with `household` null - and on 2026-09-10 chose the first, on the ground that both rules `kin[]` enforces are rules about the FAR END. The inverse must be legal; the mirror row must exist. A row with no far end is not a weaker kin row, it is one with the entire checked part removed, and a graded name with nothing checking it is a note. The second reading would also have made every genealogical name in the corpus eligible for a residents layer that reconstructs a town on one day. SO THEY ARE A NOTE, AND THEY ARE ON THE CARD: the `origin` note above names them at inferred, under this record's own Hurlbut citation, which is the idiom the `birth_year` note uses for the birthplace and hh_harmon_elijah_d and hh_porter_jeremiah use for theirs. docs/PROVENANCE.md carries the rule for the next fact that has no field, and tools/validate.py now refuses a null-household kin row in the ruling's own words rather than reporting a household that failed to resolve - a message that would send a later run off to mint a Montreal household, which is the wrong answer twice over. The evidence is unmoved, in bk_afc_004's `entities`.

persons.name: Joseph Reynolds
persons.note: A CONTEMPORARY CHICAGO PAPER OF 1833-1835 PRINTS THIS PERSON BY NAME IN THE TOWN. Read from newspaper_1833_1835. THE GRADE IS THE OWNER'S RATIFIED LADDER OF 2026-09-03 (G1b), applied to every identity at once by tools/consolidate_resident_evidence.py and spent onto this card by tools/mint_civic_residents.py; the evidence blocks below carry the reading AS READ, its locator and the record it came from, so the page can be gone back to. WHAT IS RECONSTRUCTED: everything except the person and the sources — no dwelling, no trade, no origin, no family, no party. A BOUND FROM THE RECORD, NOT AN ARRIVAL. newspaper_1833_1835 names this person at Chicago by 18 March 1834 and nothing says when they came. The bound is at or before the scene date, so the person was at Chicago by 1 July 1835 on this record's own evidence. No figure is drawn (L1). THE SECOND PRESBYTERIAN ROLL — A NAME ON A CHURCH LIST THAT OPENS IN 1842, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1892 printed membership roll of the Second Presbyterian Church of Chicago, read line by line into this repository, carries 1 line whose surname and given initial agree with this person's — “Reynolds. Mrs. J. E. | Profession. | March 2, 1844. | Dismissed.” (second_presb_0805, printed page 199), admitted 1844-03-02 by profession. Under the rule that decided it: Surname 'Reynolds' folds to the same string as the roll line's, and the given name of both begins J. WHAT THE MATCH MINTS OR REGRADES: “NOTHING. A line on a roll that opens in June 1842 cannot place a person in the town of July 1835, and this file makes no proposal that it does. What a match IS: the same surname and initial, in Chicago, within seven years — a lead for a later pass that is allowed to write people.” THE LINE IS A MARRIED WOMAN'S ENTRY, and the crosswalk's own Mrs rule governs what it can have met: “a line flagged a_married_womans_entry that meets a MAN in the 1835 layer has met his name, not him: it corroborates that the name was a Chicago name in the 1840s and it does not put that man on this roll.” The match is filed rather than suppressed, because a suppressed match is invisible and a flagged one can be argued with. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE: under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the roll is handed to the card as a thing a reader may weigh, and the verdict stays with T-0515, which applies the ladder against every source at once.

KNOWN ONLY FROM THE POST OFFICE, AND HELD THERE MORE THAN ONCE. The papers print 'Thompaon' and 'Thompsond, John' in 2 separate returns of letters uncalled-for at the Chicago post office — the Democrat of 4 March 1834, column 27; the Democrat of 20 May 1835, column 13 — across 1834-03-04 to 1835-05-20. A name in a LATER return is somebody still being written to, months on, which is the strongest thing a letter list can say about residence and is why this person outranks a single-return name of the same surname. Nothing else in the corpus names this person: no trade, no street, no household, no arrival, so every other claim here is written unattested in its own block. WHAT THAT IS WORTH: a correspondent believed a person of this name reachable at Chicago on that date, and nothing further — not that they lived here, kept a trade here, or were here on 1 July 1835. It is the weakest evidence this project accepts for a resident, and a source placing them elsewhere retires the record. THE ARGUMENT EVERY RECORD OF THIS KIND SHARES is written once instead of once per file: the ruling of 2026-08-30 and what it cost the town (docs/LIBERTIES.md L214), the refusals and the transcription standard behind the reading (tools/mint_letter_list_residents.py). No figure is drawn (L1). T-1004 — A SECOND MAN'S DEATH NOTICE CAME OFF THIS CARD. Fergus's old-settler notice `Thompson, Gen. John Leverett, lawyer, died Jan. 31, 1888, a. 53.` (fdn0666) was folded onto this person under the rule that lifts a bare forename into the one fuller name carrying it — so far that the consolidated identity was filed under the general's name rather than this man's. It is ruled off him in data/residents/card_conflation_rulings.json on the register's own arithmetic: fifty-three at a death on 31 January 1888 puts the birth about 1835, which makes him at most an infant on the scene date and not yet born when the Chicago Democrat held a letter for John Thompson on 4 March 1834. A letter list names a man who can be written to. The rank is deliberately not used as an argument here: `Lieut J L Thompson` stands on his own card and card_merge_rulings.json refuses that pair by R4, which is untouched.

FERGUS 1839'S FORT DEARBORN ADDITION LOT SALE — JUNE 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. This person bid at the sale of the Fort Dearborn Addition, 10-24 June 1839, printed in Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 at pages 47-49. The bidder is printed as “A. Wright”. 2 lot rows, $1,040 in all: block 13 lot 15 at $480 (f1839_lot0238, printed page 49); block 13 lot 16 at $560 (f1839_lot0239, printed page 49). The sale table's own shorthand, recorded and not flattened: 1 of those rows prints the bidder as a ditto mark under the name above rather than the name itself; 2 carry the block number forward from the last row that printed one. What a match may carry, and it is short: that the man was in Chicago between the 10th and the 24th of June 1839 and bid at the Fort Dearborn Addition sale. It is written as 1839 evidence with describes_date 1839-06, never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on this alone. Under the ratified ladder a second contemporary source is what lifts projected_resident, and a land sale four years after the scene date is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not about July 1835. THE LOT IS NOT A LOCATION FOR 1835: the Fort Dearborn Addition is the Beaubien, or Reservation, lands, which in July 1835 were the garrison's ground and were not platted into lots at all. It places no house, no shop and no household in the town this project builds. No trade, no address in the town of 1835, no household and no house. The block and lot are the only location on the page, they are ground platted in 1839 out of the garrison's reservation, and they place nobody in the town of 1835. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Wright' folds to the same string as the bidder's, and the given name of both begins A. (data/research/directories/fergus_1839_lots_crosswalk_1835.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a lot sale four years after the scene date is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about July 1835. self-reported addresses, which are the strongest address evidence this project has: the advertiser was paying, and his customers had to find him
dissolution, removal and replacement notices — the only thing that keeps a documented business out of the 1835 town under the owner's ruling 3
post-office letter lists, naming residents by the hundred (ruling 1: a listed name mints a resident candidate, flagged letter_list_only)
the village and later town ordinances, printed complete — the 7 November 1833 code is the richest single item in the run
arrivals and clearances, which date the piers and the harbour as working structures
public notices that fix a building as a polling place, an auction site or a meeting place on a given day
the paper's own imprint, self-reported: the corner of South Water and Clark streets
twenty-one months of continuous weekly attestation ending three weeks before the scene date, including the issue printed on 1835-07-01

the specific corner of any junction it names: 'on the corner of' does not say which of the four
anything at all from an engraving — see trap 1; the cuts are the printer's stock
proof that a business named in 1833 or 1834 still stood on 1835-07-01; that is ruling 3's survival liberty, and it is a liberty

The block, its scheduled roof count and its family mix follow the 665-roof programme; exact presence, lot, position, footprint, finish and instance-level form are interpretive. H-family house massing currently resolves through the frame dwelling archetype; no larger house generator is implemented. THE CENTRE HALL IS THE ENTRY'S, NOT THIS PARCEL'S (T-1686). H1 is the only family of the thirty-five whose crosswalk entry names a centre hall and states a bare bay count — its required variant is "center_hall_one_and_half" and its variants line reads "5 bays; center hall; kitchen ell; small porch" — so the plan and the bay count below are read off that entry and not dealt by this parcel. The kitchen ell and the small porch the same line offers are NOT raised with them: both are selectable variants beside the required one, and an ell is a footprint fact this record's rectangle does not carry.
